rows.question: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
queries: What is the notice period before filing a cheque bounce complaint?
dishonour of cheque for insufficiency of funds notice period demand payment
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 section 138 notice within thirty days
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 drawer fail to make payment of money fifteen days of receipt of said notice
rows.answer:
The notice period for making a demand for payment before filing a cheque bounce complaint is fifteen days from the date of receipt of the notice by the drawer, as stated in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [1].
- The payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment by giving a notice in writing to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid [1].
- The drawer of the cheque fails to make the payment within fifteen days of receiving the said notice [1].

rows.question: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
queries: What is presumed about consideration for a negotiable instrument?
presumption as to negotiable instruments consideration date time of acceptance transfer
Negotiable Instruments Act section 118 presumption as to consideration
Negotiable Instruments Act section 138 holder in due course consideration
rows.answer:
Every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration, according to Section 118 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 [1]. 

Conditions and time limits:
- The presumption holds until the contrary is proved [1].
- In the Supreme Court judgment "K.P.O. Moideenkutty Hajee versus Pappu Manjooran and Anr.", it was noted that Section 118 imposes a duty on the court to raise a presumption that the instrument was made for consideration, which shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to establish that the promissory note is not supported by consideration [11].

Related provisions:
- Section 43 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 covers that a negotiable instrument made, drawn, accepted, indorsed or transferred without consideration, or for a consideration which fails, creates no obligation of payment between the parties to the transaction [5].

rows.question: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
queries: When can a contract be avoided if consent was obtained by coercion or misrepresentation?
contract voidable on account of coercion fraud misrepresentation
Indian Contract Act section 19 voidability of agreements without free consent
Indian Contract Act section 15 coercion defined and section 18 misrepresentation defined
rows.answer:
When consent to an agreement is caused by coercion or misrepresentation, the agreement is a contract voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused, as stated in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. 

However, if consent was caused by misrepresentation or by fraudulent silence, the contract is not voidable if the party whose consent was so caused had the means of discovering the truth with ordinary diligence, according to the exception in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1]. Furthermore, a fraud or misrepresentation that did not cause the consent of the party on whom it was practised or to whom it was made does not render a contract voidable, as explained in Section 19 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 19A of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 covers the power to set aside a contract induced by undue influence [4].

rows.question: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
queries: Who is competent to enter into a contract?
competency to contract age of majority soundness of mind disqualified by law
Indian Contract Act section 11
Indian Contract Act section 12 what is a sound mind for the purpose of contracting
topSources: The Indian Council of World Affairs Act, 2001 s1
rows.answer:
Every person is competent to contract who is of the age of majority according to the law to which they are subject, who is of sound mind, and who is not disqualified from contracting by any law to which they are subject, as stated in Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 [1][12].

Related provisions:
- Section 10 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, covering "What agreements are contracts" [7][12][13].
- Section 12 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, covering "What is a sound mind for the purposes of contracting" [2][12][13].

rows.question: What is the punishment for murder?
queries: What is the punishment for murder?

rows.answer:
Whoever commits murder shall be punished with death or imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which replaced Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code [1][7]. 

When a group of five or more persons acting in concert commits murder on the ground of race, caste or community, sex, place of birth, language, personal belief or any other similar ground, each member of such group shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine under Section 103(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. 

Whoever, being under sentence of imprisonment for life, commits murder, shall be punished with death or with imprisonment for life, which shall mean the remainder of that person's natural life under Section 104 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [5].

queries: What is the punishment for theft?

rows.answer:
The punishment for theft under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine, or with both [1]. For a second or subsequent conviction under this section, the punishment is rigorous imprisonment for a term of not less than one year and up to five years, along with fine [1]. 

- In cases of theft where the value of the stolen property is less than five thousand rupees, and a person is convicted for the first time, upon return of the value of property or restoration of the stolen property, the punishment shall be community service [1].

Related provisions:
- Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which states that whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, is said to commit theft [1].
- Section 305 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which provides punishment for theft in a dwelling house, or means of transportation or place of worship, etc., with imprisonment of either description up to seven years and fine [5].

- Section 359 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 covers the compounding of offences relating to defamation [3].

The old law this replaced: section 499 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Defamation) [7].

rows.answer: A person accused of a non-bailable offence may be released on bail when arrested or detained without warrant by an officer in charge of a police station, or when appearing or brought before a Court other than the High Court or Court of Session, provided there do not appear reasonable grounds for believing they are guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, and provided they are not disqualified as a prior convict under the specified conditions, though the Court may direct release if the person is a child, a woman, sick, or infirm, or for other special reasons [1]. (Note: Section 480 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 is the current law; it replaced Section 437 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [1][7].) Furthermore, at any stage of investigation, inquiry, or trial, if it appears there are no reasonable grounds for believing the accused committed a non-bailable offence but there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry, the accused shall be released on bail or on executing a bond [1][12]. rows.question: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
queries: How is a sale of immovable property defined and completed?
sale of immovable property definition transfer of ownership price
Transfer of Property Act section 54 sale how made delivery of property
Transfer of Property Act section 54 contract for sale immovable property
topSources: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 s54

rows.answer:
A sale of immovable property is defined as a transfer of ownership in exchange for a price paid or promised or part-paid and part-promised, under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1]. 

As observed by the Supreme Court in Lucknow Nagar Nigam & Others versus Kohli Brothers Colour Lab. Pvt. Ltd. & Others, in order to constitute a sale, there must be a transfer of ownership from one person to another, meaning all rights and interests possessed by a person are transferred with free consent for a price called consideration, the conveyance has to be regarded in accordance with law, and title passes from the seller to the buyer only when the transaction is complete without the transferor retaining any part of their interest [11].

Conditions and time limits:
- For tangible immovable property of the value of one hundred rupees and upwards, or for a reversion or other intangible thing, the transfer can be made only by a registered instrument under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 [1].

rows.question: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
queries: What is the punishment for identity theft using a computer?
punishment for identity theft using a computer or communication device

Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita section 318 cheating by personation
topSources: The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016. s37
rows.answer:
Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly makes use of the electronic signature, password, or any other unique identification feature of any other person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to rupees one lakh under Section 66C of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [1][6][7].

Related provisions:
- Section 66D of the Information Technology Act, 2000 covers punishment for cheating by personation by using computer resource, stating that whoever by means of any communication device or computer resource cheats by personating, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine which may extend to one lakh rupees [3].

In the case of a second or subsequent conviction, the offender shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term not less than one year and up to five years, along with a fine under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1]. For a first-time conviction of theft where the stolen property's value is less than five thousand rupees, the offender shall instead be punished with community service upon the return or restoration of the stolen property's value under Section 303 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [1].
